paragraphs.section_heading: Rule 3.47 – Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 3 (Part 5)
paragraphs.text: A third party defendant may do one or more of the following: (a) apply to the Court to set aside service in accordance with rule 11.31; (b) apply to the Court for an order under rule 3.68 with respect to the third party claim; (c) apply to the Court for an order under rule 3.68 with respect to the plaintiff's statement of claim; (d) file a statement of defence or demand for notice.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.47:1 Rule 3.47 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.47. 1. Function of Rule … a plaintiff does have a right to move to set aside a third party notice. The express right given to a plaintiff by R. 68 may be in recognition of the fact that a third party becomes a de facto defendant for the purpose of disputing the defendant's liability to the plaintiff. That is, the third party can defend the plaintiff's claim against the defendant in addition to defending the defendant's claim against himself: R. 71(2). If a plaintiff can successfully have a third party notice set aside he eliminates a possible adversary in advancing his claim against the defendant. Westlands Industrial Park Ltd. v. Burgee Developments Ltd. (1982), 23 Alta. L.R. (2d) 201 at 203 (Master). 2. Application to Strike after Statement of Defence In my view, R. 68 does not preclude an application to strike a third party notice being made after a defence has been filed… The filing of a defence and the passage of time cannot legitimize a third party notice which has no foundation. Herr v. Herr (1991), 80 Alta. L.R. (2d) 328 (Q.B.) at 334, per O'Leary J. 3. Grounds for Setting Aside Rule 68 does not indicate on what grounds a third party notice can be set aside. However, as the rule deals with both a third party or a plaintiff moving to set aside the notice, logically a plaintiff should be able to rely at least on those grounds that a third party can rely on. Westlands Industrial Park Ltd. v. Burgee Developments Ltd. (1982), 23 Alta. L.R. (2d) 201 at 203 (Master). 4. If Third Party Notice Provides Full Defence to Defendant Both parties rely on Alberta Energy Co. v. Daniel Industries Inc. et al. (1990), 100 A.R. 74 (C.A.), as the leading case in this area. In Alberta Energy, supra, the Court of Appeal held that if the third party notice provides the defendant with a full answer to the plaintiff's claim, it should be struck. However, if it is possible that the third party and the defendant are jointly liable, the notice should stand. The court held at p. 75: The rule forbids a third party notice which is based solely on facts which, if proved, would give a complete defence to the main action. In such a case the very facts which would make the third party liable to the defendant would make the defendant not liable to the plaintiff. The main action would be dismissed, and there would be no need for contribution or indemnity. It is clear from Alberta Energy, supra, that if the allegations against the Crown provide an “all or nothing” answer to Burnco's [plaintiff's] claim, the third party notice is improper. Burnco Rock Products Ltd. v. Schomburg Industries (Canada) Inc. (1998), 229 A.R. 37 ((Q.B.)), at 40, per Moore C.J.Q.B. The Court of Appeal allowed an appeal from Chief Justice Moore's decision [(1998) 228 A.R. 163], but did not disagree with the above statement of law. 5. Practice of Court on Application … the court, in exercising its discretion under R. 68 of the Alberta Rules of Court, should examine the pleadings to determine whether there are common issues that might be decided differently if the indemnity proceedings were severed from the principal action. Schug v. Odegaard (1984), 32 Alta. L.R. (2d) 355 at 362 (Q.B.).

paragraphs.text: 3.49. Third party statement of defence
paragraphs.heading: Part 3. Court Actions

sentences.text: Third party statement of defence

paragraphs.text: (1) A statement of defence by a third party defendant (a) must be in Form 17, (b) must comply with the rules about pleadings in Part 13, Division 3, and (c) may dispute either or both of the following: (i) the defendant's liability to the plaintiff, or (ii) the third party defendant's liability described in the third party claim. (2) If a third party defendant files a statement of defence, the third party defendant must file it and serve it on each of the other parties within the applicable time after service of the third party claim on the third party defendant. (3) The applicable time is (a) 20 days if service is effected in Alberta, (b) one month if service is effected outside Alberta but in Canada, and (c) 2 months if service is effected outside Canada. (4) A third party defendant may do either or both of the following: (a) make a claim against a third party co-defendant in accordance with rule 3.43; (b) make a counterclaim in accordance with rule 3.56(2). Alta. Reg. 143/2011, s. 5

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.49:1 Rule 3.49 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.49. 1. Reason for Rule It is not difficult to understand the reason for the existence of the rule. The application of it prevents a defendant who may have nothing to lose by admitting liability from doing so to the prejudice of the third party who is the one who is ultimately liable … I believe that the parties who might be potentially ultimately liable should be given a full opportunity to defend both the defendants' claim against the third party, and the plaintiff's cliam against the defendant, regardless of whether the defendant admits liability to the plaintiff. I believe that this is the intention of the rule. Edmonton Savings & Credit Union Ltd. v. Wruk (1986), 45 Alta. L.R. (2d) 285 at 287-88 (Master).

paragraphs.text: 3.51. Effect of demand for notice
paragraphs.heading: Part 3. Court Actions

sentences.text: Effect of demand for notice

paragraphs.text: (1) If a third party defendant files and serves a demand for notice, the third party defendant must be served with notice of any application in which the third party defendant is named as respondent. (2) Judgment may be entered against a third party defendant who has filed and served a demand for notice only if (a) the third party plaintiff applies to the Court for judgment, and (b) notice of the application is served on the third party defendant. (3) If a third party defendant files and serves a demand for notice, the third party defendant may subsequently file a statement of defence only with the Court's permission.

paragraphs.text: 3.52. Consequences of not filing third party statement of defence
paragraphs.heading: Part 3. Court Actions

sentences.text: Consequences of not filing third party statement of defence

paragraphs.text: (1) If a third party defendant does not file a statement of defence disputing the liability of the defendant to the plaintiff, the third party defendant admits the validity of any judgment that the plaintiff obtains against the defendant, whether obtained by agreement or otherwise. (2) If a third party defendant does not file a statement of defence disputing the third party defendant's liability to the third party plaintiff under the third party claim, the third party defendant admits liability to the extent claimed in the third party claim.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.53:1 Rule 3.53 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.53. 1. Deemed admissions In Melcosky v. Maguire, 2015 ABQB 434, the third party was noted in default. Justice Read said: 108 When a party is noted in default, the claims are deemed to have been admitted and all that may be controverted is the amount of the judgment (Yaremchuk v Haight, 2001 ABCA 7 (at para 5). The amount of the judgment must be assessed unless the claim is for a debt or liquidated demand (r 3.39). In Yaremchuk v. Haight, 2001 ABCA 7, the Court said: 5 In my view, a party who is noted in default does not cease to be a party to the action and is entitled to utilize Rule 244.1. According to Rule 142(3) once a defendant has been noted in default he or she is no longer entitled to deliver a statement of defence or demand of notice. Furthermore, once the defendant has been noted in default: • [a]ll the plaintiff has to prove, or the defendant is permitted to controvert, is the amount of the damages; for the cause of action itself, as stated in the plaintiff's claim, and the right to some damages in respect of it, is admitted by the defendant, by his suffering judgement to pass against him by default. • T.W. Chitty, ed., Chitty's Archibold's Practice of the Queen's Bench Division, vol. 2, 14th ed. (London: Sweet & Maxwell, 1885) at 1336, as cited in Sulef v. Parkin and Breno (1966), 57 W.W.R. 236 (Alta. C.A.) But I have not been provided with any authority or directed to any Rule which might otherwise limit the right of a defendant to take any other step under the Rules. 2. Setting aside on failure to defend The Saskatchewan Court of Appeal, in interpreting the equivalent rule, set out several principles for setting aside the default: The general principles governing the right to set aside a default judgment apply. Lamont, J.A. (as he then was) set out these principles in Klein v. Schile, [1921] 2 W.W.R. 78, at page 79, as follows: The circumstances under which a Court will exercise its discretion to set aside a judgment regularly signed are pretty well settled. The application should be made as soon as possible after the judgment comes to the knowledge of the defendant, but more delay will not bar the application, unless an irreparable injury will be done to the plaintiff or the delay has been wilful … The application should be supported by an affidavit setting out the circumstances under which the default arose and disclosing a defence on the merits … It is not sufficient to merely state that the defendant has a good defence upon the merits. The affidavits must show the nature of the defence and set forth facts which will enable the Court or Judge to decide whether or not there was matter which would afford a defence to the action … If the application is not made immediately after the defendant has become aware that judgment has been signed against him, the affidavits should also explain the delay in making the application; and, if that delay be of long standing, the defence on the merits must be clearly established. Warner Construction Co. v. Wood River (Rural Municipality) (1979), 1 Sask. R. 118 at 119-20 (C.A.).

paragraphs.text: 3.56. Right to counterclaim
paragraphs.heading: Part 3. Court Actions

sentences.text: Right to counterclaim

paragraphs.text: (1) A defendant may, by counterclaim, file a claim against (a) a plaintiff, or (b) the plaintiff and another person whether the other person is a party to the action by the plaintiff or not. (2) A third party defendant may, by counterclaim, file a claim against the plaintiff, defendant or third party plaintiff, or any combination of them, with or without any other person, whether the other person is a party to the action or not.

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.56:1 Rule 3.56 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.56. One Cannot Add a Non-Party as Plaintiff-by-Counterclaim In Lil Dude Ranch Ltd. v. 1229122 Alberta Inc., 2014 ABQB 39, 2014 CarswellAlta 82, 5 Alta. L.R. (6th) 154 (Master), Master Robertson said, at paragraphs 29–31, and 36: 29 It is manifestly clear that the former Rule 93(1) and Rule 3.56(1) say that only a defendant can advance a counterclaim. Although the wording of the new rule is slightly different than the former rule, they both say that a defendant can advance a counterclaim, and in doing so the defendant can add other parties as defendants-by-counterclaim in addition to the plaintiff. Neither the former rule nor the current rule admit of the possibility of adding a stranger to the proceedings as a plaintiff-by-counterclaim. 30 This is what Master Alberstat said clearly in Bhatt v. Hoogstraat, [1989] A.J. No. 927, 1989 CarswellAlta 421 at paragraph 4: The rule is quite explicit. Only a defendant can file a counterclaim. There is no provision whatsoever for someone who is a stranger to the action, to file a counterclaim. The counterclaim therefore is, or was, a nullity. 31 In reaching this conclusion, he was following a decision of the Alberta Supreme Court, Appellate Division in 1957 under an earlier version of the Rules, Makarchuk v. Pollard, [1957] A.J. No. 38, 1957 CarswellAlta 77, which also described a counterclaim made by a non-party as a nullity, and a 1972 decision of the Alberta Supreme Court that had followed Makarchuk, being Saskatchewan v. Buskas, [1972] A.J. paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.59:1 Rule 3.59 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.59. 1. What Is a Counterclaim? A counter-claim is sometimes a mere set-off; sometimes it is in the nature of a cross-action; sometimes it is in respect of a wholly independent transaction. I think the true mode of considering the claim and counter-claim is, that they are wholly independent suits, which, for convenience of procedure are combined in one action. Atlantic Acceptance Corp. v. Burns & Dutton Construction (1962) Ltd., [1971] 1 W.W.R. 84 (Alta. C.A.), at 92, per Allen J.A., citing Brett L.J. in Winterfield v. Bradnum (1878), 3 Q.B.D. 324 at 326 (C.A.). The counterclaim need not relate to the main action. A defendant can counterclaim for “any claim or cause of action” against the plaintiff. The cross-claim need not be tied to or in some way relate to the main action. Phoenix Piston Hydraulics Inc. v. Echo Valley Farms Inc. (1996), 44 Alta. L.R. (3d) 283 (Master), at 287, per Master Funduk. 2. Where Parties Are Identical The counterclaim need not be related to the main action where the parties are the same. What it comes down to is that a defendant can counterclaim against the plaintiff for anything that he could have advanced by cross-action. There should not be a severance unless both the claim and the cross-claim advanced by way of counterclaim cannot be conveniently disposed of in the same action. Grenke v. Sookermany (1986), 75 A.R. 300 at 305 (Master). 3. Set-off Generally There was no set-off at common law. It was introduced into the law of England by statute … and made to apply only as between liquidated claims, although these claims may be unrelated. This is what he might call legal set-off. Equity then followed the law, and permitted a similar set-off where one of one or both of the claims was an equitable liquidated claim … This was a form of equitable set-off. Aboussafy v. Abacus Cities Ltd., [1981] 4 W.W.R. 660 (Alta. C.A.), at 670, per Kerans J.A. 4. Legal Set-Off and Equitable Set-Off In Soler & Palau Canada Inc. v. Meyer's Sheet Metal Ltd., 2012 ABQB 496, 2012 CarswellAlta 1327, 545 A.R. 391, 77 Alta. L.R. (5th) 194 (Master), Master Hanebury said, at paragraphs 48-49: 48 Legal set-off applies between liquidated claims, which is not the situation in this case: McBride v. Kolenko (1990) 115 A.R. 348, paras. 23–26 (Master), Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce v. Tucker Industries Inc., (1983) 149 D.L.R. (3d) 172, (BCCA), para. 6. 49 Equitable setoff requires that certain tests be met. The party relying on the set-off must show some equitable ground for being protected from the plaintiff's demand; the equitable ground must go to the very root of the plaintiff's claim; the cross-claim must be so clearly connected with the plaintiff's demand that it would be manifestly unjust to allow the plaintiff to enforce payment without taking the cross-claim into account; the claim and cross-claim need not arise out of the same contract; and unliquidated and liquidated claims are on the same footing: Coba Industries Ltd. v. Millie's Holdings (Canada) Ltd. And Tsang, [1985] 6 W.W.R. 14, para. 22–27; Holt v. Telford, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 193, para. 35. 5. Equitable Set-off Equitable set-off is available where there is a claim for a money sum whether liquidated or unliquidated: see Aboussafy v. Abacus Cities Ltd., [1981] 4 W.W.R. 660 (C.A.), at 666 … it is available where there has been an assignment. There is no requirement of mutuality. The authorities to be reviewed indicate that courts of equity had two rules regarding the effect of a notice of assignment on the right to set-off. First, an individual may set off against the assignee a money sum which accrued and became due prior to the notice of assignment. And second, an individual may set off against the assignee a money sum which arose out of the same contract or series of events which gave rise to the assigned money sum or was closely connected with that contract or series of events … Thus, cases involving debts that arise from the same contract or closely interrelated contracts form an exception to the general rule. In these cases a debt arising out of the contract or closely interrelated contracts may be set off against the assignee even if the debt accrues due after the notice of the assignment. Holt v. Telford, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 193, at 206, 211, per Wilson J. Master Funduk commented on equitable set-off and the decision in Holt v. Telford, [1987] 2 S.C.R. 193, in National Cabinet Lock of Canada Inc. (Assignee of) v. Steel-Craft Door Products Ltd. (1996), 44 Alta. L.R. (3d) 335 (Master). At pp. 342-43, the learned Master said: Equity recognized assignments of debts long before the common law did. (It took legislation to change the common law). As part of that recognition equity said that the assignee took the debt subject to the equities between the assignor and the debtor. But that rule is not an unlimited rule. Anything and everything between the assignor and the debtor was not considered to be “equities” for the purpose of the rule. There are boundaries to the rule. That is the thrust of the last sentence of the above quote from Telford. There had to be a connection of some sort between the “equity” raised by the debtor and the assigned debt. In Royal Bank v. Wilton (1995), 28 Alta. L.R. (3d) 1; [leave to appeal to S.C.C. refused 32 Alta. L.R. (3d) xliv], the Court of Appeal reviewed the five elements necessary for equitable set-off. At p. 13 the court said: The five elements cited by the Supreme Court of Canada in Holt were taken from the case of Coba Industries Ltd. v. Millie's Holdings (Canada) Ltd., [1985] 6 W.W.R. 14 (B.C. C.A.). Specifically the five elements are as follows [p. 22]: 1) The party relying on the set-off must show some equitable ground for being protected against his adversary's demands… 2) The equitable ground must go to the very root of the plaintiff's claim before a set-off will be allowed… 3) A cross claim must be so clearly connected with the demand of the plaintiff that it would be manifestly unjust to allow the plaintiff to enforce payment without taking into consideration the cross-claim… 4) The plaintiff's claim and the cross-claim need not arise out the same contract… 5) Unliquidated claims are on the same footing as liquidated claims… 6. Set-off and Counterclaim Are Different Set-off must be distinguished from cross-claim. Both are available by counterclaim under R. 93. Set-off provides a defence to a claim but cross-claim does not …Canadian Commercial Bank (Liquidator of) v. Parlee McLaws (1989), 64 Alta. L.R. (2d) 218 (Q.B.), at 221, per Wachowich J., citing with approval Aboussafy v. Abacus Cities Ltd., [1981] 4 W.W.R. 660 (C.A.). In P.P.G. Canada Inc. v. Alberta Window Manufacturing Inc. (1998), 235 A.R. 54 (Master), Master Funduk said, at p. 57: The rule does not make all counterclaims a defence of set-off. Set-off, to be a defence, must be legal set-off or equitable set-off … In Aboussafy v. Abacus Cities Ltd., [1981] 4 W.W.R. 660 (Alta. C.A.), Kerans J.A. said at p. 670: … By set-off is meant something in the way of a defence: where claim and cross-claim are merged and the lesser is thereby extinguished. True set-off must be distinguished from procedural set-off, where two unrelated claims are balanced up and a net judgment given: see Stooke v. Taylor (1880), 5 Q.B.D. 569 … Procedural set-off is a shield, not a sword. It is not a defence; it therefore is not an equity subject to which an assignee takes. Unlike a true set-off, there is no charge against the fund of the original chose in action which equity can recognize. And Master Funduk said: To equate set-off with counter-claim is an error. Subrules (1) and (2) of rule 93 do not mean the same thing. Subrule (1), as between the original parties, merely embodies s. 17(3)(a) [of the Judicature Act], while subrule (2) dictates how a particular kind of defence is to be raised in a pleading. Grenke v. Sookermany (1986), 75 A.R. 300 at 305 (Master). 7. Legal Set-off Legal set-off “requires the fulfilment of two conditions. The first is that both obligations must be debts. The second is that both debts must be mutual cross obligations. Both conditions must be fulfilled at the same time”: C.I.B.C. v. Tuckerr Indust. Inc., [1983] 5 W.W.R. 602 at 604 (C.A.) (approved in Holt v. Telford at p. 204). Any assignment of the debts destroys mutuality and precludes the operation of legal set-off: Holt v. Telford at p. 205. Canadian Commercial Bank (Liquidator of) v. Parlee McLaws (1989), 64 Alta. L.R. (2d) 218 at 222 (Q.B.).

paragraphs.text: 3.60. Application of rules to counterclaims
paragraphs.heading: Part 3. Court Actions

sentences.text: Application of rules to counterclaims

paragraphs.text: (1) Except when the context or these rules otherwise provide, a rule that applies to or in respect of (a) a plaintiff applies equally to or in respect of a plaintiff-by-counterclaim and a third party plaintiff-by-counterclaim, (b) a defendant applies equally to or in respect of a defendant-by-counterclaim and a third party defendant-by-counterclaim, and (c) a pleading related to a claim made by statement of claim applies equally to or in respect of a pleading related to a counterclaim. (2) If the defendant-by-counterclaim does not file a statement of defence or demand for notice in respect of a counterclaim, a judgment on the counterclaim may be obtained only with the Court's permission after notice of the application has been served on the defendant-by-counterclaim.

(a) a plaintiff applies equally to or in respect of a plaintiff-by-counterclaim and a third party plaintiff-by-counterclaim

(c) a pleading related to a claim made by statement of claim applies equally to or in respect of a pleading related to a counterclaim.

paragraphs.text: 3.61. Request for particulars
paragraphs.heading: Part 3. Court Actions

sentences.text: Request for particulars

paragraphs.text: (1) A party on whom a pleading is served may serve on the party who served the pleading a request for particulars about anything in the pleading. (2) If the requesting party does not receive a sufficient response within 10 days after the date on which the request is served, the requesting party may apply to the Court for an order requiring the party who served the pleading to provide the particulars. (3) If the Court orders particulars to be provided, it must specify a time within which the order is to be complied with. sentences.text: (1) A party on whom a pleading is served may serve on the party who served the pleading a request for particulars about anything in the pleading.

(2) If the requesting party does not receive a sufficient response within 10 days after the date on which the request is served, the requesting party may apply to the Court for an order requiring the party who served the pleading to provide the particulars.
(3) If the Court orders particulars to be provided, it must specify a time within which the order is to be complied with.

(4) Subject to any order, despite a request for particulars, the obligation under these rules to file and serve pleadings continues even though a request for particulars has been made and whether or not it has been complied with.

When Available Particulars generally will not be ordered after the close of pleadings and before discovery. The timing of this application also gives me some difficulty. While the primary purpose of particulars is to enable to the other side to defend, particulars may also serve to narrow the issues, prevent surprise at trial and save time. To accomplish this, particulars may be ordered after the close of the pleadings. (See Anglo-Canadian Timber Products Ltd. v. British Columbia Electric Co. Ltd., supra; Okalta Oils Limited v. Alberta Petroleum Consolidated Limited, [1935] 2 W.W.R. 664 (Alta. S.C.); Odgers on Pleading and Practice (21st Ed.), p. 149). In my view, the law on this point is correctly summarized in Canadian Encyclopedic Digest (Western, 2nd Ed.), vol. 17, at para. 106, as follows: Particulars are ordered primarily with a view of having the prior pleading made sufficiently distinct to enable the applicant for particulars to frame his answer properly. If the pleadings are closed particulars cannot be required for that purpose, but, notwithstanding the pleadings are closed, particulars may be ordered, in a proper case, for the purpose of saving expense, or for the purpose of preventing surprise at the trial. The proper principle is to order particulars only when, from the nature of the case, they are necessary to limit the inquiry, or are necessary by reason of matters brought forward on affidavit. It is now well-settled practice that particulars after pleading will not be ordered until after discovery; following this principle further, if discovery results in full disclosure, particulars are not necessary; if discovery does not result in full disclosure particulars will be ordered. It follows that discovery takes the place of particulars if it results in full disclosure. To justify an order for particulars after the close of the pleadings, it must be shown by affidavit, or otherwise, that they are necessary for the purpose of saving expense or preventing surprise at the trial. Such an order should not be made as of course. Oceatain Investments Ltd. v. Canadian Commercial Bank (1983), 51 A.R. 364 (Q.B.), at 366-67, per McFadyen J. (approved by Prowse J. in Magrath Market Place Ltd. v. 401624 Alberta Inc. (1991), 83 Alta. L.R. (2d) 94 at 96 (Q.B.)). Particulars may be ordered after examinations for discovery if that process has been unsuccessful in providing the information: This is not the usual case of a party applying for particulars. The pleadings are closed and the plaintiff was content to go to discoveries with the pleas as they stand. The plaintiff expected to get better particulars on discovery. If he had got what he wanted on discoveries this application would not have been made. A party cannot say that better particulars of his pleas should not be given because the pleadings are closed, and also say that better particulars should not be given on discoveries. That reduces itself to saying that better particulars should not be given at any time. The other party must wait to trial to see what the particulars are. That of course would not be acceptable. The fact that the defendant has refused to give more particulars at its examination is a special circumstance to justify the ordering of particulars if the pleading is deficient in that regard. Here discovery of the officer has not resulted in full disclosure so particulars should be ordered: Oceatain Investments v. Canadian Commercial Bank (1983), 51 A.R. 364 (Q.B.) …Caskey v. Guardian Insurance Co. of Canada (1994), 148 A.R. 251 (Master), at 257, per Master Funduk. 2. Entitlement to Particulars Defendants are entitled to particulars even if the defendant has the information. Counsel for the plaintiff submits that the defendants have knowledge of how this figure is arrived at as they were formerly his solicitors. I do not believe that this is an appropriate position. The plaintiff is advancing a claim for loss of income against the defendants. They are entitled to know how he arrives at that amount. Kully v. Decore (1981), 34 A.R. 617 at 620 (Master). In Stoney Tribal Council v. R., 2005 ABCA 204, 2005 CarswellAlta 773, 54 Alta. L.R. (4th) 184, the Court said, at pp. 185-186: The appellant (the new defendant) formally demanded a number of particulars of the amended statement of claim. The respondent plaintiffs refused to provide almost all the particulars demanded, alleging in each case that they were “evidence in the possession and control of the Defendants” or the like. The reply to demand for particulars did not allege that the appellant (the new defendant) had such knowledge. It is admitted that the appellant was incorporated about 70 years after the C.P.R.'s original line was built. In any event, the fact that a defendant knows the facts is not a legal objection to the plaintiff's giving particulars. That is because particulars are pleadings and claims, not discovery or evidence. For example, the defendant driver in a highway collision suit was present at the collision and saw it all, but he is still entitled to particulars of the plaintiff's plea of negligence. The defendant may know what he actually did, but he does not know what the plaintiff thinks that the defendant did. It is no objection to an application for particulars that the applicant must know the true facts of the case better than his opponent. He is entitled to know the outline of the case that his adversary will try to make against him, which may be something very different from the true facts of the case. • Goulding, Simon, Odgers on Civil Court Actions, p. 215, 24th ed. (London: Sweet & Maxwell, 1996) And if a statement of claim covers a large topic or more than one specified transaction, the defendant does not know which of the many things which he has done is in issue. Nor whether the complaint is something which someone else did, or no one did. The question is one of natural justice: notice of the claim which the defendant has to meet. We are persuaded by the reasoning to like effect in Kully v. Decore (1981), 34 A.R. 617 (Alta. Q.B.), 620 (M.) (para. 7), and in Caskey v. Guardian Insurance Co. of Canada (1994), 148 A.R. 251 (Alta. Master), 255-6 (M.) (para. 29). (There is a contrary statement in Misericordia Hospital v. Acres Consulting Services Ltd. (1977), 5 A.R. 254 (Alta. T.D.), but it gives no reasoning and cites Patterson v. Canadian Pacific Railway (1917), [1918] 1 W.W.R. 40 (Alta. C.A.). That case is not on point, and very likely pp. 45-46 of it have been misread.) If the provision of particulars will unduly delay the action, the court may decline to order them. In most cases, it is undoubtedly true that a defendant is entitled to know all the facts (not evidence) of the case against him before he is required to plead. However, this case is unique, from the point of view of the number of defendants, the complexity of the the issues involved, the quantum of damages claimed and the massive quantities of relevant documents (estimated by the plaintiffs to be in the neighbourhood of two million pages). I accept the plaintiff's argument that if they were required to supply exhaustive particulars at this stage, the proceedings would be substantially delayed, perhaps by as much as one year. No one would be able to proceed with discovery of documents or examinations for discovery until the plaintiffs had completed and finalized their list of particulars… I also agree with the defendants' submission that examination for discovery are no substitute for particulars, since one of the functions of particulars is to narrow the issues and thus circumscribe the scope of discoveries. There is a danger that the defendants will be put to unnecessary time and expense in they are not given complete particulars at this stage. However, there is an overriding factor in the litigation. Because of the magnitude of the alleged liability, I am certain that each defendant will conduct thorough and lengthy discoveries. After examining all the material before me, I am satisfied that all defendants are presently in possession of sufficient particulars to enable them to plead and to get started on what is certain to be an extremely lengthy discovery process. Canadian Commercial Bank (Liquidator of) v. McLaughlan (1988), 62 Alta. L.R. (2d) 362 (Q.B.), at 366-67, per Wachowich J. Justice Wachowich's decision in Canadian Commercial Bank (Liquidator of) v. McLaughlan (1988), 62 Alta. L.R. (2d) 362 (Q.B.), should not be taken as authority to provide only partial particulars when consequential delay is not an issue. In 1021018 Alberta Ltd. v. Bazinet, 2015 ABQB 151, the Plaintiff sought “damages and other relief against Mr. Bazinet and four other Defendants, for loss of business revenue due to alleged activities of the Defendants which allegedly sought to harm the reputation of the Plaintiff. Specifically, the Plaintiff [alleged] improper use of the Plaintiff's confidential information and trade secrets.” The Defendant Bazinet demanded particulars. The Plaintiff filed and served a Notice to Admit Facts. In the Plaintiff's reply to the Defendant's demand for particulars, the Plaintiff used the phrase “includes but not limited to”. Justice Schutz did not approve the use of that phrase: 37 As for the phrase “includes but not limited to”, Wachowich J expresses concern about this qualifier in Canadian Commercial Bank, and notes that questioning is not a substitute for particulars. In that case, however, Wachowich J did not order further particulars because he was satisfied that “… all Defendants are at present in possession of sufficient particulars to enable them to plead and to get started on with what is certain to be an extremely lengthy discovery process”: Canadian Commercial Bank at para 33. 38 The Plaintiff must give the Defendant particulars of what the Plaintiff knows. Mr. Bazinet is not obliged to speculate, or guess, about what the Plaintiff knows. Accordingly, the Plaintiff shall remove references to what the Defendant “knows” and replace those references with such further or other particulars upon which the Plaintiff intends to rely in its case against Mr. Bazinet. 39 Further, the phrase “including but not limited to” shall not form part of the Plaintiff's pleadings. I agree that in the face of an allegation “including but not limited to”, questioning cannot and shall not be a substitute for particulars, and I am not able to find that Mr. Bazinet is at present in possession of sufficient particulars to enable him to sufficiently plead his defence or prepare evidence for questioning, or trial. 40 Relevance is determined by the pleadings. The Plaintiff's intention to rely on allegations that the Defendant “knows”, or that some allegations are “including but not limited to” other, unstated, unknown allegations, is not fair to the Defendant. The boundaries of the Plaintiff's pleadings must be drawn with sufficient particularity by the Plaintiff that the Defendant is not left to speculate, or guess, about that to which the Plaintiff refers, or about the case the Defendant must meet. 41 I find that the Plaintiff's particulars, to this point, suffer the same frailties as the deficiencies mentioned in Stoney and Caskey and Canadian Commercial Bank: Mr. Bazinet is entitled to know the outline of the case that his adversary will try to make against him, which may be something very different from the true facts of the case. The amended statement of claim covers a large topic and more than one specified transaction. By using phrases such as “on or about [a given date]”, “further particulars of every defamatory statement are available to Bazinet but not [the Plaintiff]”, “further particulars are known to Bazinet”, I agree that it is not possible for Mr. Bazinet to know which of the many things he has done is in in issue. Nor is Mr. Bazinet able to know whether the Plaintiff's complaints are actually about something which someone else did, or no one did. I agree that the fundamental question is one of natural justice: notice of the claim which the defendant has to meet. 3. Purpose of Particulars In Gulf Canada Ltd. v. “Mary Mackin” (The), [1984] 1 F.C. 884, 42 C.P.C. 146, 52 N.R. 282 (C.A.), at 284, Heald J. approved the following as an accurate list of the functions of particulars (as taken from the White Book dealing with English Practice): 1. to inform the other side of the nature of the case they have to meet as distinguished from the mode in which that case is to be proved; 2. to prevent the other side from being taken by surprise at the trial; 3. to enable the other side to know what evidence they ought to be prepared with and to prepare for trial; 4. to limit the generality of the pleadings; 5. to limit and decide the issues to be tried, and as to which discovery is required, and 6. to tie the hands of the party so that he cannot without leave go into any matters not included. Moshansky J., in Welco Expediting Ltd. v. Harris (1995), 31 Alta. L.R. (3d) 173 (Q.B.), at 181-82, referred with approval to that list. And McFadyen J. stated: The function of particulars is stated in Halsbury's Laws of England (4th Ed.), vol. 36, para. 38, as follows: The function of particulars is to carry into operation the overriding principle that the litigation between the parties, and particularly the trial, should be conducted fairly, openly and without surprises, and incidentally to reduce costs. This function has been variously stated, namely either to limit the generality of the allegations in the pleadings, or to define the issues which have to be tried and for which discovery is required. Each party is entitled to know the case that is intended to be made against him at the trial, and to have such particulars of this opponent's case as will prevent him from being taken by surprise. Particulars enable the other party to decide what evidence he ought to be prepared with and to prepare for the trial. The general rule is that an application for particulars must be accompanied by an affidavit disclosing the applicants' need for particulars. An affidavit is unnecessary where the allegations are so general and so vague that the need for particulars is evident. (See Anglo-Canadian Timber Products Ltd. v. British Columbia Electric Co. Ltd. (1960), 23 D.L.R. (2d) 656 (B.C. C.A.) and Steiner v. Lindzon et al. (1976), 1 C.P.C. 237 (Ont. H.C.J.). Oceatain Investments Ltd. v. Canadian Commercial Bank (1983), 51 A.R. 364 at 366 (Q.B.). In Alberta v. Altria Group, Inc., 2015 ABQB 390, Justice Strekaf gave this overview of the purpose of particulars and the test to be met in an application for particulars: 14 The purpose of particulars has been discussed in numerous decisions. Any request for particulars should be considered in light of the principle that each party is entitled to know the case that is intended to be made against it at trial. Particulars help to ensure that litigation is conducted fairly, openly, and without surprise. Particulars also help to narrow the scope of the issues to be decided, guide the discovery process, and help to streamline the litigation process. 15 A request for particulars is not akin to an examination for discovery. Particulars function to limit the generality of allegations and to define the issues to be tried, whereas examinations for discovery are to learn the knowledge of the adverse party: Misericordia Hosp v Acres Consulting Services Ltd (1977), 5 AR 254 at 255 (ABSC-TD) (Misericordia). … 17 While not mandatory, an application for particulars should as a general rule be accompanied by an affidavit disclosing the applicant's need for particulars. No substantive affidavits were filed on behalf of any of the Defendants in this case. Therefore, to show that particulars are required, absent an affidavit stating as such, the Defendants must show that the pleading is defective on its face and that “the allegations are so general and so vague that the need for particulars is evident”: Oceatain Investments Ltd v Canadian Commercial Bank (1983), 51 AR 364 (ABQB) at para 8 (Oceatain). 18 The Court has discretion in determining whether the allegations are so vague as to necessitate an order for particulars. As noted by Justice McMahon in Re Indian Residential Schools, 1999 ABQB 823 at para 15: • An order for particulars is discretionary. There are no precise rules as to the degree of particularity required in any given case. Generally, what is reasonable and fair will dictate whether, and to what degree, further particulars will be ordered. 19 Justice McMahon noted that there is a difference between ordering particulars for pleadings and ordering particulars for trial. For an order for particulars in order to plead, the court should ask itself: “are there sufficient facts present to formulate a defence?” This question must be answered with reference to the whole of the Crown's Statement of Claim: see Wesley First Nation v Alberta, 2009 ABQB 418 at para 34 (Wesley First Nation). 20 Pleadings must be succinct, but must still disclose sufficient material facts for the defendant to understand what case it must meet. The amount of detail necessary varies with the nature of each case: William Blake Odgers, Principles of Pleadings and Practice in Civil Actions, 21st ed (London: Stevens & Sons, 1975) at 103. If a specific fact is not set out, but can be properly inferred from other statements in the pleading, that is sufficient for the purposes of a statement of claim: see O'Neill v Rosetown (Town), [1941] 2 WWR 481 (SKCA). 21 Pleadings require facts, but should not contain evidence. The line between these is often difficult to draw: see Can-Air Services Ltd v British Aviation Insurance Co (1988), 63 Alta LR (2d) 61 (CA). Material facts are facts upon which the party pleading relies for its claim, whereas evidence consists of the manner by which those facts are to be proved: Misericordia. The distinction between the two is often a question of degree. Expert report or opinion is evidence, not material fact, and therefore need not be particularized: Hoy v Medtronic, 2004 BCSC 440 at para 39. 22 Finally, requests for particulars that are in the nature of a question of law or of mixed fact and law need not be answered: see Commonwealth Credit Union Ltd v Waylan Mechanical Ltd, 2008 ABQB 96. iv)—Particulars in Complex Cases 23 What degree of particularity is “reasonable and fair” will depend on the circumstances of the case. Various courts have recognized that a realistic and pragmatic approach should be adopted at the pleadings stage in very complex litigation to ensure that these cases are not unduly delayed or prevented from proceeding to trial. This approach is exemplified by the reasoning of the Court of Appeal in Lameman v Alberta, 2013 ABCA 148 at para 29 (Lameman): • A plaintiff is required to sufficiently particularize its claim so as to permit the defendants to identify their defenses for the purpose of filing a Statement of defense. However, the demands for particulars should not be permitted to turn into a delaying tactic, or a substitute for what can be obtained through a Notice to Produce Records or the Questioning process Otherwise, litigation will be stonewalled at an early stage through excessive particularization. 24 This approach is reflected in other Alberta cases. In Re Indian Residential Schools, Justice McMahon held that the court should have a view to the “magnitude and nature of the litigation involved” in determining what, if any, particulars should be ordered: para 16. In Re Indian Residential Schools, Justice McMahon was considering an application for particulars in a case involving over one thousand actions, over two thousand complainants, and multiple defendants for alleged abuses spanning seven decades. Justice McMahon concluded that, in cases of such size and complexity, “potential delay must be an overriding consideration”: para 18. The courts must adopt a “reasonable and realistic” approach, “seeking fairness for all parties”: paras 16, 21. On one hand, the court should help the parties to narrow the issues as much as possible before discovery. On the other hand, any order for particulars cannot be “so onerous as to prevent Plaintiffs from prosecuting an action which is meritorious …”: para 16. Justice McMahon therefore addressed the issue of potential delay by ordering particulars in a staggered fashion: he ordered broad particulars on a representative basis in order to help the Defendants to frame their defenses and noted that many of the requests would be addressed in discovery. 25 In Wesley First Nation, Justice Martin was similarly considering an application for particulars in a large and complex case where the “claims are extensive, the breaches alleged are numerous, the relevant time frame spans hundreds of years and the territory at issue is vast”: para 2. In this context, Justice Martin endorsed this “realistic” approach at para 23: • While recognizing the need for defendants to understand the case made against them at the pleadings stage, the court must also recognize that not every claim is capable of being pleaded with the same degree of particularity, and that subsequent stages in the litigation process may also function to clarify and narrow the issues. 26 While courts must avoid unduly burdening the plaintiff in its claims, there is a risk that the discovery process will become unwieldy and unnecessarily time-consuming and costly if insufficient particularization is given to the claims. 27 To strike a balance between these competing considerations in large and complex litigation, case management judges “must have some elbow room” in order to “keep the suit moving” and prevent it from being “[bogged] down in interlocutory matters”: Korte v Deloitte, Haskins & Sells (1995), 36 Alta LR (3d) 56 (CA) at para 3. The Court of Appeal in Lameman noted that in complex cases that are case managed, litigation management orders can be more effective than particulars in providing an efficient structure to determine a claim: para 32. 4. Function of Particulars In my view, the guiding principle is that the primary purpose of particulars is to enable the other side to frame a defence. The pleadings should be as succinct as is reasonably possible in order to achieve this end. In Balaz v. Petro-Infor Ltd. (1983), 43 A.R. 229 at 233, the Alberta Court of Appeal dismissed one of a number of applications for further and better particulars in the following way: In my view the allegations with regard to conspiracy, although somewhat vague, are of sufficient particularity to enable the appellants to answer in defence. However, this is not the only function of particulars. They also serve to narrow the issues for trial and to save time and expense in the trial preparation process and in the trial. In Lougheed v. C.B.C., [1979] 3 W.W.R. 334 at 352 … the Alberta Court of Appeal held: The defendant is entitled to such particulars as are reasonably necessary for its defence, both in respect of pleading and the steps leading to trial as well as the conduct of the trial itself. Mr. Justice Hope sets out an excellent summary of the purposes of providing particulars in Misericordia Hosp. v. Acres Consulting Services Ltd. (1977), 5 A.R. 254 at 255 (T.D.): In summary, those principles insofar as I see they apply to this application are: (a) The function of particulars is to limit the generality of allegations and define the issues to be tried—whereas examinations for discovery is to learn the knowledge of the adverse party; (b) Particulars do not include the facts within the knowledge of the applicant; (c) Particulars are not required to be given of the character of the act which it is alleged produced the damage nor the circumstances under which it is done; (d) A distinction is made between particulars of the ‘material fact’ stated generally in the Statement of Claim as ‘facts on which the party pleading relies for his claim’ and which he must state and particulars of the ‘evidence by which they are to be proved’. There is a fine line between providing sufficient particulars to enable a defendant to plead, and pleading evidence. The latter is specifically prohibited by R. 104, which states that the pleadings shall contain the material facts on which the party is relying, but not the evidence by which they are to be proved. In most cases, it is undoubtedly true that a defendant is entitled to know all the facts (not evidence) of the case against him before he is required to plead. Canadian Commercial Bank (Liquidator of) v. McLaughlan (1988), 62 Alta. L.R. (2d) 362 (Q.B.), at 365-66, per Wachowich J. In Geophysical Service Incorporated v. Plains Midstream Canada ULC, 2021 ABCA 55, 2021 CarswellAlta 278, the Court said: [5]“Particulars” are, by definition, further details about the claim originally pleaded. If they go beyond that, they are potentially “new” claims which must comply with s. 6(2). A plaintiff cannot indirectly add new claims to a proceeding by describing them as particulars. Further, if the particulars are merely evidence in support of the original claim, they are not a proper part of the pleading; pleadings are to allege facts, but not include evidence: R. 13.6(2)(a). 5. Particulars of Damages I will now deal with the issue of the particulars of damages. I agree with the submission by the defendants Clarkson Gordon and Peat Marwick that the plaintiffs must be required to give particulars of any special damages that they are claiming, so that the defendants are in a position to properly contest the quantum. According to Odgers' Principles of Pleadings and Practice, 22nd ed. (1981), p. 154: Particulars of general damages will very rarely be ordered. But when any special damage is claimed without sufficient detail, particulars will be ordered of the alleged damage, e.g. if the plaintiff alleges that certain customers have ceased to deal with him, he will be ordered to state their names. This is a very useful order, for if a plaintiff cannot give the names, he will be compelled to strike out the allegations of special damage; and the summons should ask that it be struck out if such particulars be not delivered. If he gives the necessary particulars he will be bound by them; he will not be allowed at the trial to give evidence of any special damage which is not claimed explicitly, either in his pleadings or particulars. If ambiguous expressions be used in the statement of claim which may or may not amount to allegations of special damage, the master will order ‘particulars of special damage, if any claimed.’ The first thing that must be considered, therefore, is whether the claim for $294,000,000 is for special or general damages. The distinction between special and general damages was laid down by Lord Macnaghten in Stroms Bruks Aktie Bolag v. Hutchinson, [1905] A.C. 515 at 525-56: ‘General damages’, as I understand the term, are such as the law will presume to be the direct, natural and probable consequence of the act complained of. ‘Special damages,’ on the other hand, are such as the law will not infer from the nature of the act. They do not follow in the ordinary course. They are exceptional in their character, and, therefore, they must be claimed specifically and proved strictly. Canadian Commercial Bank (Liquidator of) v. McLaughlan (1988), 62 Alta. L.R. (2d) 362 at 369 (Q.B.).

Master), 255-6 (M.) (para.
(There is a contrary statement in Misericordia Hospital v.
Acres Consulting Services Ltd.
254 (Alta.
T.D.), but it gives no reasoning and cites Patterson v.
Canadian Pacific Railway (1917), [1918] 1 W.W.R.
40 (Alta.
That case is not on point, and very likely pp.
45-46 of it have been misread.) If the provision of particulars will unduly delay the action, the court may decline to order them.
In most cases, it is undoubtedly true that a defendant is entitled to know all the facts (not evidence) of the case against him before he is required to plead.

However, this case is unique, from the point of view of the number of defendants, the complexity of the the issues involved, the quantum of damages claimed and the massive quantities of relevant documents (estimated by the plaintiffs to be in the neighbourhood of two million pages).
I accept the plaintiff's argument that if they were required to supply exhaustive particulars at this stage, the proceedings would be substantially delayed, perhaps by as much as one year.

No one would be able to proceed with discovery of documents or examinations for discovery until the plaintiffs had completed and finalized their list of particulars… I also agree with the defendants' submission that examination for discovery are no substitute for particulars, since one of the functions of particulars is to narrow the issues and thus circumscribe the scope of discoveries.
There is a danger that the defendants will be put to unnecessary time and expense in they are not given complete particulars at this stage.
However, there is an overriding factor in the litigation.
Because of the magnitude of the alleged liability, I am certain that each defendant will conduct thorough and lengthy discoveries.

After examining all the material before me, I am satisfied that all defendants are presently in possession of sufficient particulars to enable them to plead and to get started on what is certain to be an extremely lengthy discovery process.
Canadian Commercial Bank (Liquidator of) v.
McLaughlan (1988), 62 Alta.
L.R.
(2d) 362 (Q.B.), at 366-67, per Wachowich J.
Justice Wachowich's decision in Canadian Commercial Bank (Liquidator of) v.
McLaughlan (1988), 62 Alta.
L.R.
(2d) 362 (Q.B.), should not be taken as authority to provide only partial particulars when consequential delay is not an issue.
In 1021018 Alberta Ltd. v.
Bazinet, 2015 ABQB 151, the Plaintiff sought “damages and other relief against Mr.
Bazinet and four other Defendants, for loss of business revenue due to alleged activities of the Defendants which allegedly sought to harm the reputation of the Plaintiff.
Specifically, the Plaintiff [alleged] improper use of the Plaintiff's confidential information and trade secrets.” The Defendant Bazinet demanded particulars.
The Plaintiff filed and served a Notice to Admit Facts.
In the Plaintiff's reply to the Defendant's demand for particulars, the Plaintiff used the phrase “includes but not limited to”.

Justice Schutz did not approve the use of that phrase: 37 As for the phrase “includes but not limited to”, Wachowich J expresses concern about this qualifier in Canadian Commercial Bank, and notes that questioning is not a substitute for particulars.

In that case, however, Wachowich J did not order further particulars because he was satisfied that “… all Defendants are at present in possession of sufficient particulars to enable them to plead and to get started on with what is certain to be an extremely lengthy discovery process”: Canadian Commercial Bank at para 33.
38 The Plaintiff must give the Defendant particulars of what the Plaintiff knows.
Mr.
Bazinet is not obliged to speculate, or guess, about what the Plaintiff knows.

Accordingly, the Plaintiff shall remove references to what the Defendant “knows” and replace those references with such further or other particulars upon which the Plaintiff intends to rely in its case against Mr.
Bazinet.
39 Further, the phrase “including but not limited to” shall not form part of the Plaintiff's pleadings.
I agree that in the face of an allegation “including but not limited to”, questioning cannot and shall not be a substitute for particulars, and I am not able to find that Mr.
Bazinet is at present in possession of sufficient particulars to enable him to sufficiently plead his defence or prepare evidence for questioning, or trial.
40 Relevance is determined by the pleadings.

The Plaintiff's intention to rely on allegations that the Defendant “knows”, or that some allegations are “including but not limited to” other, unstated, unknown allegations, is not fair to the Defendant.

The boundaries of the Plaintiff's pleadings must be drawn with sufficient particularity by the Plaintiff that the Defendant is not left to speculate, or guess, about that to which the Plaintiff refers, or about the case the Defendant must meet.
41 I find that the Plaintiff's particulars, to this point, suffer the same frailties as the deficiencies mentioned in Stoney and Caskey and Canadian Commercial Bank: Mr.
Bazinet is entitled to know the outline of the case that his adversary will try to make against him, which may be something very different from the true facts of the case.
The amended statement of claim covers a large topic and more than one specified transaction.

By using phrases such as “on or about [a given date]”, “further particulars of every defamatory statement are available to Bazinet but not [the Plaintiff]”, “further particulars are known to Bazinet”, I agree that it is not possible for Mr.
Bazinet to know which of the many things he has done is in in issue.
Nor is Mr.
Bazinet able to know whether the Plaintiff's complaints are actually about something which someone else did, or no one did.
I agree that the fundamental question is one of natural justice: notice of the claim which the defendant has to meet.
Purpose of Particulars In Gulf Canada Ltd. v. “Mary Mackin” (The), [1984] 1 F.C.

282 (C.A.), at 284, Heald J. approved the following as an accurate list of the functions of particulars (as taken from the White Book dealing with English Practice): 1. to inform the other side of the nature of the case they have to meet as distinguished from the mode in which that case is to be proved; 2. to prevent the other side from being taken by surprise at the trial; 3. to enable the other side to know what evidence they ought to be prepared with and to prepare for trial; 4. to limit the generality of the pleadings; 5. to limit and decide the issues to be tried, and as to which discovery is required, and 6. to tie the hands of the party so that he cannot without leave go into any matters not included.
Moshansky J., in Welco Expediting Ltd. v.
Harris (1995), 31 Alta.
L.R.
(3d) 173 (Q.B.), at 181-82, referred with approval to that list.
And McFadyen J. stated: The function of particulars is stated in Halsbury's Laws of England (4th Ed.), vol.
36, para.

38, as follows: The function of particulars is to carry into operation the overriding principle that the litigation between the parties, and particularly the trial, should be conducted fairly, openly and without surprises, and incidentally to reduce costs.
This function has been variously stated, namely either to limit the generality of the allegations in the pleadings, or to define the issues which have to be tried and for which discovery is required.
Each party is entitled to know the case that is intended to be made against him at the trial, and to have such particulars of this opponent's case as will prevent him from being taken by surprise.
Particulars enable the other party to decide what evidence he ought to be prepared with and to prepare for the trial.
The general rule is that an application for particulars must be accompanied by an affidavit disclosing the applicants' need for particulars.
An affidavit is unnecessary where the allegations are so general and so vague that the need for particulars is evident.
(See Anglo-Canadian Timber Products Ltd. v.
British Columbia Electric Co.
Ltd.
C.A.) and Steiner v.
Lindzon et al.
Oceatain Investments Ltd. v.
Canadian Commercial Bank (1983), 51 A.R.
In Alberta v.

Altria Group, Inc., 2015 ABQB 390, Justice Strekaf gave this overview of the purpose of particulars and the test to be met in an application for particulars: 14 The purpose of particulars has been discussed in numerous decisions.
Any request for particulars should be considered in light of the principle that each party is entitled to know the case that is intended to be made against it at trial.
Particulars help to ensure that litigation is conducted fairly, openly, and without surprise.
Particulars also help to narrow the scope of the issues to be decided, guide the discovery process, and help to streamline the litigation process.
15 A request for particulars is not akin to an examination for discovery.

Particulars function to limit the generality of allegations and to define the issues to be tried, whereas examinations for discovery are to learn the knowledge of the adverse party: Misericordia Hosp v Acres Consulting Services Ltd

(1977), 5 AR 254 at 255 (ABSC-TD) (Misericordia). … 17 While not mandatory, an application for particulars should as a general rule be accompanied by an affidavit disclosing the applicant's need for particulars.
No substantive affidavits were filed on behalf of any of the Defendants in this case.

Therefore, to show that particulars are required, absent an affidavit stating as such, the Defendants must show that the pleading is defective on its face and that “the allegations are so general and so vague that the need for particulars is evident”: Oceatain Investments Ltd v Canadian Commercial Bank
(1983), 51 AR 364 (ABQB) at para 8 (Oceatain).
18 The Court has discretion in determining whether the allegations are so vague as to necessitate an order for particulars.
As noted by Justice McMahon in Re Indian Residential Schools, 1999 ABQB 823 at para 15: • An order for particulars is discretionary.
There are no precise rules as to the degree of particularity required in any given case.
Generally, what is reasonable and fair will dictate whether, and to what degree, further particulars will be ordered.
19 Justice McMahon noted that there is a difference between ordering particulars for pleadings and ordering particulars for trial.

For an order for particulars in order to plead, the court should ask itself: “are there sufficient facts present to formulate a defence?” This question must be answered with reference to the whole of the Crown's Statement of Claim: see Wesley First Nation v Alberta, 2009 ABQB 418 at para 34 (Wesley First Nation).
20 Pleadings must be succinct, but must still disclose sufficient material facts for the defendant to understand what case it must meet.
The amount of detail necessary varies with the nature of each case: William Blake Odgers, Principles of Pleadings and Practice in Civil Actions, 21st ed (London: Stevens & Sons, 1975) at 103.

If a specific fact is not set out, but can be properly inferred from other statements in the pleading, that is sufficient for the purposes of a statement of claim: see O'Neill v Rosetown (Town), [1941] 2 WWR 481 (SKCA).
21 Pleadings require facts, but should not contain evidence.
The line between these is often difficult to draw: see Can-Air Services Ltd v British Aviation Insurance Co (1988), 63 Alta LR (2d) 61 (CA).
Material facts are facts upon which the party pleading relies for its claim, whereas evidence consists of the manner by which those facts are to be proved: Misericordia.
The distinction between the two is often a question of degree.
Expert report or opinion is evidence, not material fact, and therefore need not be particularized: Hoy v Medtronic, 2004 BCSC 440 at para 39.

22 Finally, requests for particulars that are in the nature of a question of law or of mixed fact and law need not be answered: see Commonwealth Credit Union Ltd v Waylan Mechanical Ltd, 2008 ABQB 96. iv)—Particulars in Complex Cases 23 What degree of particularity is “reasonable and fair” will depend on the circumstances of the case.

Various courts have recognized that a realistic and pragmatic approach should be adopted at the pleadings stage in very complex litigation to ensure that these cases are not unduly delayed or prevented from proceeding to trial.

This approach is exemplified by the reasoning of the Court of Appeal in Lameman v Alberta, 2013 ABCA 148 at para 29 (Lameman): • A plaintiff is required to sufficiently particularize its claim so as to permit the defendants to identify their defenses for the purpose of filing a Statement of defense.

However, the demands for particulars should not be permitted to turn into a delaying tactic, or a substitute for what can be obtained through a Notice to Produce Records or the Questioning process Otherwise, litigation will be stonewalled at an early stage through excessive particularization.
24 This approach is reflected in other Alberta cases.

In Re Indian Residential Schools, Justice McMahon held that the court should have a view to the “magnitude and nature of the litigation involved” in determining what, if any, particulars should be ordered: para 16.

In Re Indian Residential Schools, Justice McMahon was considering an application for particulars in a case involving over one thousand actions, over two thousand complainants, and multiple defendants for alleged abuses spanning seven decades.
Justice McMahon concluded that, in cases of such size and complexity, “potential delay must be an overriding consideration”: para 18.
The courts must adopt a “reasonable and realistic” approach, “seeking fairness for all parties”: paras 16, 21.
On one hand, the court should help the parties to narrow the issues as much as possible before discovery.
On the other hand, any order for particulars cannot be “so onerous as to prevent Plaintiffs from prosecuting an action which is meritorious …”: para 16.

Justice McMahon therefore addressed the issue of potential delay by ordering particulars in a staggered fashion: he ordered broad particulars on a representative basis in order to help the Defendants to frame their defenses and noted that many of the requests would be addressed in discovery.

25 In Wesley First Nation, Justice Martin was similarly considering an application for particulars in a large and complex case where the “claims are extensive, the breaches alleged are numerous, the relevant time frame spans hundreds of years and the territory at issue is vast”: para 2.

In this context, Justice Martin endorsed this “realistic” approach at para 23: • While recognizing the need for defendants to understand the case made against them at the pleadings stage, the court must also recognize that not every claim is capable of being pleaded with the same degree of particularity, and that subsequent stages in the litigation process may also function to clarify and narrow the issues.

26 While courts must avoid unduly burdening the plaintiff in its claims, there is a risk that the discovery process will become unwieldy and unnecessarily time-consuming and costly if insufficient particularization is given to the claims.

27 To strike a balance between these competing considerations in large and complex litigation, case management judges “must have some elbow room” in order to “keep the suit moving” and prevent it from being “[bogged] down in interlocutory matters”: Korte v Deloitte, Haskins & Sells
(1995), 36 Alta LR
(3d) 56 (CA) at para 3.

The Court of Appeal in Lameman noted that in complex cases that are case managed, litigation management orders can be more effective than particulars in providing an efficient structure to determine a claim: para 32.
Function of Particulars In my view, the guiding principle is that the primary purpose of particulars is to enable the other side to frame a defence.
The pleadings should be as succinct as is reasonably possible in order to achieve this end.
In Balaz v.
Petro-Infor Ltd.

229 at 233, the Alberta Court of Appeal dismissed one of a number of applications for further and better particulars in the following way: In my view the allegations with regard to conspiracy, although somewhat vague, are of sufficient particularity to enable the appellants to answer in defence.
However, this is not the only function of particulars.
They also serve to narrow the issues for trial and to save time and expense in the trial preparation process and in the trial.
In Lougheed v.

334 at 352 … the Alberta Court of Appeal held: The defendant is entitled to such particulars as are reasonably necessary for its defence, both in respect of pleading and the steps leading to trial as well as the conduct of the trial itself.
Mr.
Justice Hope sets out an excellent summary of the purposes of providing particulars in Misericordia Hosp. v.
Acres Consulting Services Ltd.
254 at 255 (T.D.): In summary, those principles insofar as I see they apply to this application are:
(a) The function of particulars is to limit the generality of allegations and define the issues to be tried—whereas examinations for discovery is to learn the knowledge of the adverse party
(b) Particulars do not include the facts within the knowledge of the applicant
(c) Particulars are not required to be given of the character of the act which it is alleged produced the damage nor the circumstances under which it is done

(d) A distinction is made between particulars of the ‘material fact’ stated generally in the Statement of Claim as ‘facts on which the party pleading relies for his claim’ and which he must state and particulars of the ‘evidence by which they are to be proved’.
There is a fine line between providing sufficient particulars to enable a defendant to plead, and pleading evidence.
The latter is specifically prohibited by R.
104, which states that the pleadings shall contain the material facts on which the party is relying, but not the evidence by which they are to be proved.
In most cases, it is undoubtedly true that a defendant is entitled to know all the facts (not evidence) of the case against him before he is required to plead.
Canadian Commercial Bank (Liquidator of) v.
McLaughlan (1988), 62 Alta.
L.R.
(2d) 362 (Q.B.), at 365-66, per Wachowich J.
In Geophysical Service Incorporated v.
Plains Midstream Canada ULC, 2021 ABCA 55, 2021 CarswellAlta 278, the Court said: [5]“Particulars” are, by definition, further details about the claim originally pleaded.
If they go beyond that, they are potentially “new” claims which must comply with s.
A plaintiff cannot indirectly add new claims to a proceeding by describing them as particulars.
Further, if the particulars are merely evidence in support of the original claim, they are not a proper part of the pleading; pleadings are to allege facts, but not include evidence: R.
Particulars of Damages I will now deal with the issue of the particulars of damages.

I agree with the submission by the defendants Clarkson Gordon and Peat Marwick that the plaintiffs must be required to give particulars of any special damages that they are claiming, so that the defendants are in a position to properly contest the quantum.
According to Odgers' Principles of Pleadings and Practice, 22nd ed.
154: Particulars of general damages will very rarely be ordered.

But when any special damage is claimed without sufficient detail, particulars will be ordered of the alleged damage, e.g. if the plaintiff alleges that certain customers have ceased to deal with him, he will be ordered to state their names.

This is a very useful order, for if a plaintiff cannot give the names, he will be compelled to strike out the allegations of special damage; and the summons should ask that it be struck out if such particulars be not delivered.

If he gives the necessary particulars he will be bound by them; he will not be allowed at the trial to give evidence of any special damage which is not claimed explicitly, either in his pleadings or particulars.

If ambiguous expressions be used in the statement of claim which may or may not amount to allegations of special damage, the master will order ‘particulars of special damage, if any claimed.’ The first thing that must be considered, therefore, is whether the claim for $294,000,000 is for special or general damages.
The distinction between special and general damages was laid down by Lord Macnaghten in Stroms Bruks Aktie Bolag v.
Hutchinson, [1905] A.C.

515 at 525-56: ‘General damages’, as I understand the term, are such as the law will presume to be the direct, natural and probable consequence of the act complained of. ‘Special damages,’ on the other hand, are such as the law will not infer from the nature of the act.
They do not follow in the ordinary course.
They are exceptional in their character, and, therefore, they must be claimed specifically and proved strictly.
Canadian Commercial Bank (Liquidator of) v.
McLaughlan (1988), 62 Alta.
L.R.

sentences.text: Amending pleading

paragraphs.text: (1) A party may amend the party's pleading, including an amendment to add, remove, substitute or correct the name of a party, as follows: (a) before pleadings close, any number of times without the Court's permission; (b) after pleadings close, (i) for the addition, removal, substitution or correction of the name of a party, with the Court's prior permission in accordance with rule 3.74, or (ii) for any other amendment, with the Court's prior permission in accordance with rule 3.65; (c) despite clauses (a) and (b), whether or not pleadings have closed, with the agreement of the parties filed with the Court. (2) An amended pleading must be (a) filed, and (b) served on each of the other parties (i) within 10 days after the date on which it is filed, or (ii) if the pleading is a statement of claim that has not already been served, in accordance with Division 3, Subdivision 2. (3) A party may, without the Court's permission, amend that party's pleading before or after pleadings close if that amended pleading is (a) a statement of defence in response to an amended statement of claim, an amended counterclaim or an amended third party claim, or (b) a reply to an amended statement of defence, amended statement of defence to an amended counterclaim, or amended statement of defence to an amended third party claim. (4) A response pleading referred to in subrule (3) must be (a) filed, and (b) served on each of the other parties within 10 days after the date that the amended pleading referred to in subrule (3) is served. (5) If a party has pleaded in response to a pleading that is subsequently amended and served on that party and the party does not file and serve a further response to the amended pleading, the party is assumed to rely on the party's unamended pleading in response to the amended pleading referred to in subrule (3). (6) This rule does not apply to amendments to a class proceeding under the Class Proceedings Act. Alta. Reg. 163/2010, s. 2; 143/2011, s. 6
