sentences.text: Amending pleading

paragraphs.text: Commentary § 3.62:1 Rule 3.62 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.62. 1. Admissions In Korte v. Cormie (1996), 36 Alta. L.R. (3d) 431 (C.A.), the Court of Appeal defined “admissions” and indicated, without deciding, that admissions most likely cannot be made in a statement of claim. However, if admissions can be made in a statement of claim, and if they are true admissions, then they may be removed from the statement of claim only with leave. At p. 436, Madam Justice Hunt, speaking for the court said: The Rules do not define “admission”, but there are a number of Rules dealing with admissions, including RR. 25, 71, 119, 162, 165, 219, 230 and 231. These Rules tend to support the view taken by the respondents, namely, that admissions must be responsive to a statement found in pleadings. For example, R. 119 is to the effect that the silence of a pleading “as to any allegation contained in the previous pleading of the opposite party” shall not be taken to be an admission as to the truth of the allegation. Rule 25 concerns acceptance of service of an admission by the solicitor of a party. Rule 162 deals with “admissions of fact” that have been made upon the pleadings. Rules 230 and 231 set out a process for calling upon a party to admit specific facts… It seems to me that, while these cases concerned statements made in Statements of Claim, the statements which were sought to be withdrawn were of much clearer effect than the words sought to be withdrawn here. I do not find it necessary to decide whether it is ever possible to have an admission in a Statement of Claim, although in the face of the Rules mentioned above I am inclined to the view that it is not. Assuming, however, that it is possible to make an admission in a Statement of Claim, such that leave to withdraw it would be required, in this case I agree with the view of the chambers judge that what was sought to be withdrawn is not an admission but “an allegation in the framing of an action”. It is not so unambiguous as to constitute an admission. Thus, in any event, no leave to amend would be required on this ground. [Pleadings in the action had not yet closed.] 2. Amendments after Pleadings Close In Remington Development Corporation v. Enmax Power Corporation, 2022 ABCA 71, the Court of Appeal set out the test for amending pleadings, and made a specific comment about the difference between “hopeless” and “arguable”. The Court said: [33] Assuming some modest amount of evidence is provided in support, any pleading may be amended no matter how careless or dilatory the party seeking the amendment, subject to four exceptions: (1) the amendment would cause serious prejudice not compensable in costs; (2) the amendment is hopeless; (3) unless permitted by statute the pleading seeks to add a new party or cause of action after the expiry of a limitation period; or (4) there is an element of bad faith associated with the failure to plead the amendment in the first place: Attila Dogan Construction and Installation Co Inc v AMEC Americas Limited, 2014 ABCA 74 at para 25. [34] Attila Dogan posited several things that might make a proposed amendment hopeless. These included amendments which do not disclose a cause of action or where the proposed amendment is so inconsistent with the record that it could fairly be described as hopeless: at para 27. [35] Recently, in Swaleh v Lloyd, 2020 ABCA 18 this Court described the test for determining whether a plea is hopeless at para 13: An amendment to add a pleading should not be granted where the claim is hopeless, such that the pleading would have been struck if originally pled: McCargar v Métis Nation of Alberta Association, 2017 ABQB 692 at para 7, aff’d 2018 ABCA 144. A pleading is hopeless only if it is clear and obvious that there is no triable issue: McCargar at para 19. Hopelessness is met if the claim is barred by statute: see for example, Bouvry Exports Calgary Ltd v ING Insurance Company of Canada, 2008 ABQB 61. [36] In articulating the applicable test, the chambers judge at para 33 said, “I think a proposed amendment is hopeless where it is not ‘arguable’.” … [37] There is a difference between the test enunciated by this Court and that articulated by the chambers judge. “Arguable” implies that there are two possible interpretations or conclusions based upon a set of facts; in other words, there is a triable issue. Hopelessness asks if it is plain and obvious that there is no triable issue. . . . . . [41] The chambers judge did not articulate the correct test when she equated hopelessness with whether something was arguable. … 3. Amendments and Limitation Issues In Kydd v. Abolarin, 2011 ABQB 690, 2011 CarswellAlta 1980, 520 A.R. 250, Justice Macklin had before him an appeal from a Master's decision which had permitted amendments to be made to a Statement of Claim. The proposed defendant contended that the applicable limitation period had expired, and his Lordship, at paragraph 19, discussed the approach the Court should adopt in the face of such a contention: 19 In Dow Chemical Canada Inc v. Nova Chemicals Corporation, 2010 ABQB 524, Wittmann C.J. summarized the options for a Court when an amendment is sought and there is a limitations issue: 1. Determine the limitation period has not expired and allow the amendment. 2. Rule the limitation period has expired and therefore consider s 6 of the Limitations Act which provides for when an amendment can be made beyond the limitation period. 3. Find that because of uncertainty in the evidence, the amendments should be allowed subject to the determination of the limitation issue at trial … (Dow Chemical at para. 64). 4. Amendments after Limitation Period I am satisfied that a Court in Alberta, when considering amendments to statements of claim where intervening limitation periods have accrued to the benefit of the defendant, must determine whether or not the interests of justice warrant such an amendment. It must further determine whether the principles underlying the imposition of the limitation period have been affected, including the question of whether the defendant has been prejudiced by the failure of the plaintiff to include in the statement of claim the amendments sought. The burden of showing such prejudice, as in the renewal and next step cases, rests with the defendant…Dumaine v. Kerry (1988), 87 A.R. 70 at 77 (Q.B.). The prejudice spoken of is not the loss of the statutory defence of a limitation period but rather prejudice related to the merits (e.g., loss of evidence, change in the status quo, etc.). The prejudice suffered may well be the raison d'être of the limitation period. However the existence of the limitation period without more does not necessarily prove that the raison d'être exists in a given case. In Korte v. Cormie (1996), 36 Alta. L.R. (3d) 431 (C.A.), Hunt J.A., speaking for the Court of Appeal, said at p. 443: I am of the view that if an amendment raises the possibility of a limitation argument, leave of the Court should be required to amend. This is so because the inability to rely upon a limitation argument may work prejudice upon the party against whom the amendment is sought. As such, it is a situation that falls outside the broad language of R. 130. The judge hearing such an application for leave to amend has a number of choices. He or she may agree that the new claim is out of time and thus disallow the amendment; may determine that the sort of special circumstances referred to in [Basarsky v. Quinlan, [1972] S.C.R. 380] exist, and allow the amendment nevertheless; or decide that the limitation argument is of the kind that ought to be determined at trial, upon a factual base. 5. Adding a Counterclaim In Crystal Ridge Fuels Ltd. v. McIntosh, 2013 ABQB 618, 2013 CarswellAlta 2000, 573 A.R. 102, 100 Alta. L.R. (5th) 378, Justice Jones said, at paragraph 17: 17 As noted in Marlborough Ford Sales Ltd v. Ford Motor Co of Canada, 2003 ABQB 298, 13 Alta LR (4th) 336 at para 9, the effect of a counterclaim being conjoined with the statement of defence is that a defendant “must bring an application to amend his or her pleadings to add a counterclaim.” This Court also viewed an application to bring a counterclaim as an amendment to the statement of defence in Deuruneft Deutsche-Russische Mineralol Handelsgesellschaft mbH v. Bullen 2002 ABQB 304, 310 AR 164 at para 26. I conclude that adding a counterclaim engages the procedure under Rule 3.62 and, subsequently, either Rule 3.65 or Rule 3.74. 6. General comment on amendments In MTM Commercial Trust v. Statesman Riverside Quays Ltd., 2022 ABCA 328, 2022 CarswellAlta 2819, Justice Slatter made these observations: [32] The granting or denial of an amendment does not necessarily say anything about the merits of the underlying claim or the relevance of any issues raised. Subject to a very few exceptions, the denial of an amendment also does not create an issue estoppel about the issue in the pleading. For example, pleadings are sometimes disallowed because the limitation period has expired. paragraphs.text: 3.65. Permission of Court to amendment before or after close of pleadings
paragraphs.heading: Part 3. Court Actions

sentences.text: Permission of Court to amendment before or after close of pleadings

paragraphs.text: (1) Subject to subrule (5), before or after close of pleadings, the Court may give permission to amend a pleading. (2) If the Court gives permission for a pleading to be amended, the Court must specify the time period within which the amended pleading must be filed and served. (3) An order giving permission to amend a pleading under this rule ceases to have effect unless the amended pleading is filed and served within the time specified by the Court. (4) If the Court directs or allows a pleading to be amended at trial, (a) the amendment must be recorded in writing by the court clerk, and (b) no order need be filed. (5) This rule does not apply to an amendment to a pleading to add, remove, substitute or correct the name of a party to which rule 3.74 applies.
